newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Deregulation seen key to Czech inflation outlook.
newsitem.headline: Deregulation seen key to Czech inflation outlook.

text.p: Czech finance ministry plans to deregulate energy prices would keep inflation high in the long term and changes to the consumer price basket could push it to 9.5 percent in 1997, Zivnostenska Banka said on Tuesday.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Monday January monthly inflation was 1.2 percent, putting the year-on-year rate at 7.4 percent, down from 8.6 percent in December.

But a report by Zivnostenska Banka said that the January figure was skewed by the absence of traditional January price deregulation which should be be factored back into inflation calculations later in the year.
"Last January's inflation was influenced to a large extent by the price deregulation, while the same does not apply for this year's figure," the report said.
Last month, the finance ministry proposed radical deregulation of electricity, gas and heating prices over the next two years.

Under the proposals electricity prices would rise by 35 percent in 1997 and 32 percent in 1998. Gas would rise by the same amount this year and 21 percent next year. Heating would rise by 39 percent in 1997 and 10 percent in 1998.
When items directly linked to housing are taken into account, Zivnostenska Banka says deregulation would add 3.6 percentage points of "non-core" inflation to the headline figure.
"With a 3.6 percent contribution by a non-core inflation, this year's CPI index would hardly fall below eight percent even under the assumption of a stable koruna exchange rate."
The report also warned that inflation may be even higher in 1997 if finance ministry proposals to raise value added tax on energy prices to 22 percent from five percent are implemented.
A further blow to government hopes of reining in inflation could come if the CSU revised the consumer price basket to take into account the proposed price rises.
When the current basket was created in 1993, housing, which also comprises energy prices, accounted for 14.4 percent of its weighting, low by European standards.

If a new basket were created to reflect increased housing prices that weighting would rise to 20.2 percent pushing average inflation in 1997 to 9.5 percent and falling back slightly to 8.7 percent in 1998, the bank estimates.
"It is evident that inflation will remain a problem of the Czech economy for quite a long time, which does not give good prospects for an early interest rate decline."
